projects.title: Hydro-Risk Price Forecasting Model
projects.tagline: Regime-sensitive modelling of NZ wholesale electricity price risk, showing tail risk roughly doubles once hydro storage drops into the bottom decile.
projects.org: Massey University — Master of Analytics Capstone (Paper 115.801)

businessProblem.context: New Zealand's wholesale electricity price is heavily exposed to hydro storage conditions, but that exposure isn't linear — a small change in storage can mean a very different price-risk environment depending on where storage sits relative to historical norms. Wellington Electricity needed a way to see that regime shift coming rather than reacting to it after prices had already spiked.
goals: Build a regime-sensitive model linking hydro storage, tributary inflows, HVDC transfer flows, spill volumes, and climate indicators to wholesale price risk.
Quantify how tail risk (VaR/CVaR) changes specifically once storage falls into a low-storage regime, rather than assuming a constant relationship.
Turn the regime signal into an early-warning indicator that procurement and risk teams can act on ahead of price moves.
painPoints: Monthly storage, inflow, spill, HVDC and climate data lived across nine separate source folders with inconsistent formats, requiring a full standardisation and validation pass before any modelling could start.
A single linear regression across all storage levels masked what was actually happening — the real risk was concentrated in a specific low-storage regime, not spread evenly across the range.
HVDC transfer data limited the reliable estimation window to 1996-2019 (241 months), which had to be handled carefully rather than just running the model on all 279 available months of price data.

approach.methodology: Standardised and merged nine separate data sources into a single monthly panel (1996-2024, 279 observations), then classified each month into a storage regime using percentile thresholds — with the low-storage regime defined as national active storage at or below the 10th percentile (~34% of active capacity). Estimated OLS regression models with HC3 robust standard errors, moving from a simple storage-only model (R² = 0.167) to a multi-driver model adding HVDC flow, spill, lagged inflow anomaly and lagged price (R² = 0.704), then validated the storage threshold non-parametrically with a spline basis. Computed Value-at-Risk and Conditional VaR at the 95th and 99th percentiles separately for the normal and low-storage regimes to quantify tail-risk amplification, and tested a short-horizon early-warning specification to flag regime entry ahead of time.
dataSources: National hydro storage levels (active storage, % of capacity)

insights: Mean wholesale price under low-storage conditions was $300.96/MWh, versus $173.58/MWh in normal conditions and $140.97/MWh in high-storage conditions — the low-storage regime alone explains most of the price variation the model captures.
In dry-year proxy months, mean price was $438.16/MWh versus $165.21/MWh in normal months — more than double, and a materially bigger gap than the broader low-storage regime shows on its own.

Tail risk moves more than the mean does: 95th-percentile VaR jumps from $717.97/MWh (normal) to $2,026.16/MWh (low storage), and CVaR95 rises from $1,511.22 to $2,118.51 — roughly a 40% increase in expected loss beyond the 95th percentile once storage crosses the low-storage threshold.

The storage effect is non-linear: a simple storage-only regression explains little (R² = 0.167), but adding an explicit low-storage interaction term (coefficient -20.656, p < 0.001) and lagged drivers (HVDC flow, spill, inflow anomaly, lagged price) lifts explanatory power to R² = 0.704, with lagged price the strongest single driver — evidence that price shocks persist rather than resetting each month.

recommendations: Use the ~34%-of-capacity storage threshold as a hedge-escalation trigger — a concrete, monitorable line rather than a qualitative 'storage is getting low' judgement call.

Size hedging and procurement buffers off CVaR95 by regime, not off the unconditional average price — the ~40% jump in expected tail loss under low storage is the number that actually matters for exposure planning.

Because lagged price is the strongest driver in the multi-driver model, treat a live price spike as informative about near-term persistence, not just a one-off data point, when deciding whether to escalate hedging.

Extend the early-warning specification (built on a 3-month-ahead dry-regime flag) into a monitoring routine that flags regime entry before storage fully crosses the threshold, giving procurement a lead-time advantage rather than a reactive one.
projects.roi: Quantified that expected tail-loss exposure (CVaR95) rises roughly 40% once hydro storage falls into the bottom decile, and identified a concrete, monitorable storage threshold (~34% of active capacity) that can anchor a hedge-escalation trigger rather than relying on qualitative judgement.

codeSnippets.title: Tail-Risk: VaR & CVaR by Regime
codeSnippets.code:
def var_cvar(x, q=0.95):
    x = pd.Series(x).dropna().values
    v = np.percentile(x, 100*q)
    c = x[x >= v].mean() if (x >= v).any() else np.nan
    return v, c

rows = []
for label, subset in [("Normal", tail_df[tail_df["LowStorage_10"]==0]),
                      ("LowStorage_10", tail_df[tail_df["LowStorage_10"]==1])]:
    v95, c95 = var_cvar(subset["Price_mean"], 0.95)
    v99, c99 = var_cvar(subset["Price_mean"], 0.99)
    rows.append({
        "Regime": label,
        "n": len(subset),
        "VaR95": v95,
        "CVaR95": c95,
        "VaR99": v99,
        "CVaR99": c99
    })

tail_risk_by_regime = pd.DataFrame(rows)

projects.title: Credit Risk Segmentation & Customer Clustering
projects.tagline: Reducing 18 behavioural credit variables to 3 components, then segmenting 30,000 clients into risk archetypes validated at 94.5% accuracy.
projects.org: Massey University — Multivariate Analysis for Big Data

businessProblem.context: Lenders typically score credit risk with a single blended number, which hides the fact that two clients with the same score can be risky for completely different reasons — one is over-extended but pays on time, another has modest balances but keeps missing payments. This project used the UCI 'Default of Credit Card Clients' dataset (30,000 Taiwanese credit card accounts, April–September 2005) to test whether behavioural segmentation could surface those distinctions.
goals: Identify the underlying behavioural factors that actually drive default, rather than treating 18 monthly variables as independent inputs.
Determine whether distinct client archetypes exist based on financial behaviour.
Test how reliably those archetypes can be classified — i.e. whether the segmentation is statistically real or just visually plausible.
painPoints: The 18 repayment-status, bill-amount and payment-amount variables across six months are heavily correlated with each other, so feeding them into a model directly creates redundancy and multicollinearity.
Running hierarchical clustering on all 30,000 observations was computationally impractical in SAS and produced a dendrogram with completely unreadable axis labels.
A clustering result on its own proves nothing — it needed independent validation to show the groups were genuinely separable.

approach.methodology: Cleaned and standardised the dataset (z-score transformation across all 18 continuous variables; unknown education codes retained as an explicit 'Unknown' category rather than dropped, to preserve completeness). Ran Principal Component Analysis to reduce the 18 correlated variables to three interpretable components. Used those components as inputs to hierarchical clustering via Ward's minimum variance method, on a stratified sample of 1,000 clients (500 defaulters, 500 non-defaulters) — a deliberate trade-off after the full 30,000-observation run proved unreadable and computationally slow. Finally validated the resulting clusters with Linear Discriminant Analysis using PROC DISCRIM with cross-validation enabled, testing whether clients could be correctly re-classified into their assigned cluster.
dataSources: UCI 'Default of Credit Card Clients' dataset — 30,000 accounts, 6 months of demographic, billing, repayment and default data

insights: Three principal components captured ~79% of total variance (PC1 41.13%, PC2 23.21%, PC3 14.48%), and each had a clear behavioural meaning: PC1 = overall credit usage volume, PC2 = delinquency/payment delay, PC3 = repayment consistency.

Clustering on those components produced three distinct client archetypes: high financial activity with timely payments (low-risk), delayed payments with low repayment amounts (high-risk), and moderate activity with inconsistent payment behaviour (middle tier).

Discriminant analysis confirmed the segmentation held up: 94.6% resubstitution accuracy and 94.5% cross-validated accuracy, with a cross-validated error rate of roughly 5.5% — the clusters are statistically separable, not an artefact of the clustering method.

Clients who defaulted tended to have lower credit limits, and clients with lower or unknown education levels showed the highest default rates — suggesting a link between financial literacy and credit behaviour worth exploring further.

visualizations.description: Clients who defaulted show a visibly lower credit limit distribution than those who did not.

visualizations.title: Scree Plot of Principal Components
visualizations.description: A clear elbow at the third component — after PC3 each additional component contributes very little, supporting a three-component solution.

recommendations: Use the three validated archetypes as the basis for risk-based pricing tiers rather than a single blended score — the drivers of risk differ meaningfully between groups.
Prioritise the delinquency component (PC2) as an early-warning signal, since it isolates payment-delay behaviour from sheer credit usage volume.
For datasets of this size, prefer PCA scatterplots over dendrograms for communicating cluster structure — the dendrogram becomes visually unusable well before it becomes analytically useless.
Re-run the segmentation periodically, as behavioural patterns shift with economic conditions.
projects.roi: Reduced 18 correlated credit variables to 3 interpretable behavioural dimensions and produced a three-segment client model validated at 94.5% cross-validated classification accuracy — a defensible basis for risk-based pricing and targeted credit policy.

projects.title: Financial Hardship Modelling
projects.tagline: Two-stage econometric study of 14,669 survey respondents testing whether everyday financial habits actually protect against hardship — and for whom.

businessProblem.context: Financial hardship policy tends to treat behaviours like budgeting and goal-setting as universally protective. But whether those habits actually help — and how much — plausibly depends on who you are: your income, marital status, employment, and education. This two-part study tested that directly, first modelling hardship as a continuous score, then as a set of concrete hardship events (selling possessions, missing rent, needing welfare).
goals: Quantify how financial capability, gambling harm, income and demographics jointly drive financial hardship.
Test whether the protective effect of financial habits varies across subgroups, using interaction terms rather than assuming a uniform effect.
Establish that findings survive diagnostic checks — heteroscedasticity, multicollinearity, and goodness-of-fit — before drawing any policy conclusion.
painPoints: Hardship scores are heavily right-skewed: most respondents report little to no hardship, with a long tail of severe distress — so the average tells you very little about the people who actually need help.
The behavioural, demographic and income predictors are correlated with each other, making it hard to isolate any single factor's contribution.
Interaction effects are easy to over-interpret; several plausible-sounding hypotheses needed to be tested and honestly reported as unsupported.

approach.methodology: Stage 1 (Assessment 1): estimated an Ordinary Least Squares regression of a continuous financial hardship score on financial capability, gambling harm, their interaction, income (including a squared term to capture non-linearity), and demographic controls. Tested the full set of Classical Linear Regression Model assumptions — linearity, normality of residuals, homoscedasticity and multicollinearity — then re-estimated with Huber-White robust standard errors to confirm coefficients held. Stage 2 (Assessment 2): reframed hardship as three binary outcomes — selling or pawning possessions, missing rent or mortgage, and relying on welfare — and estimated four logistic regression models, each pairing a financial behaviour with a demographic moderator via an interaction term. Assessed each model on AIC, concordance (c-statistic) and the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test.
dataSources: Survey of 14,669 respondents across 31 variables covering financial behaviours, socio-demographics and hardship experiences

insights: Financial capability significantly reduced hardship, but gambling harm significantly increased it — and the interaction was significant, meaning gambling erodes the protective benefit of financial literacy rather than acting independently of it.

Financial monitoring significantly reduced the odds of selling or pawning possessions (p = 0.0003), and the interaction with marital status was significant (p = 0.0326) — the protective effect was stronger for married respondents, pointing to shared household financial decision-making.

Not every plausible interaction held. Goal-setting × education (p = 0.2152), monitoring × employment (p = 0.5248), and goal-setting × income (p = 0.1614) were all non-significant — the behaviours help broadly, but not measurably more for those specific subgroups.

The OLS model explained ~16% of hardship variance (R² = 0.1619, F(12, 14227) = 228.96, p < 0.0001) — modest in absolute terms but typical for behavioural models where individual circumstance dominates.

All four logistic models exceeded a c-statistic of 0.72, with the welfare-reliance model performing best at 0.829, and all passed the Hosmer–Lemeshow test — indicating well-calibrated, reliable classification.

visualizations.title: Distribution of Financial Hardship Scores
visualizations.description: Heavily right-skewed: most respondents report zero or minimal hardship, with a long tail of severe distress that the mean alone would obscure.

visualizations.title: Gambling Harm by Respondent Group
visualizations.description: Most respondents report little to no gambling harm, with a small number of significant outliers.

visualizations.title: Predicted Probability of Asset Liquidation by Marital Status
visualizations.description: As financial monitoring increases, the predicted probability of selling or pawning possessions falls — and the decline differs by marital status, which is the significant interaction the model identified.

recommendations: Pair financial monitoring programmes with joint household planning tools for couples — that's where the interaction shows the effect is strongest.
Treat gambling harm as a direct threat to financial capability programmes, not a separate issue: it measurably erodes the benefit those programmes are designed to deliver.

Don't over-target by education, employment or income when promoting goal-setting and monitoring — the data shows these habits help broadly, so narrow eligibility criteria would exclude people who benefit.
Use the welfare-reliance model (c = 0.829) as the strongest of the four for identifying at-risk individuals proactively.
projects.roi: Produced a diagnostically validated two-stage model of financial hardship across 14,669 respondents, identifying which financial behaviours protect against hardship, which subgroup differences are real, and — equally usefully — which widely assumed subgroup effects are not statistically supported.

projects.title: Inside-Out Performance: Aligning CRM Wins with Real-World Demand
projects.tagline: Enriching a B2B CRM pipeline with Google Trends and scraped GPU benchmarks to test whether top-selling products are actually winning — or just thriving in a bubble.
projects.org: Massey University — Data Mastery: Scripting, Databases and Data Privacy

businessProblem.context: Internal CRM dashboards tell you which products close deals. They don't tell you whether anyone outside the company has heard of them. This project started from one question about a B2B computer hardware pipeline: are our top-selling products genuinely aligned with market demand, or succeeding in a closed loop where internal sales effort — not external demand — is doing the work?
goals: Establish which CRM products actually perform, measured by conversion rate rather than raw deal count.
Bring in independent external signals — public search interest and third-party hardware benchmarks — to test internal performance against outside reality.
Build a composite score combining internal and external evidence to segment products into High, Mid and Low performers for strategic decisions.
painPoints: CRM data is self-referential: a product can look healthy internally while being invisible to the wider market, and nothing in the CRM would reveal that.

External signals had to be acquired from different sources in different shapes — Google Trends API pulls and web-scraped benchmark tables — then aligned to CRM products and time periods before any comparison was possible.
Deal duration was skewed by a small number of very long negotiations, which distorted downstream analysis until capped.

approach.methodology: Wrangled the CRM sales pipeline (accounts, products, sales teams, opportunities), capping deal durations above the 95th percentile to control skew. Ran exploratory analysis across conversion rates, deal stages, agent performance, account size and seasonality, then tested four internal hypotheses covering agent performance variation, account size versus deal value, agent seniority, and deal duration versus conversion. Enriched the internal picture with three external sources: Google Trends search interest for product and category keywords, GPU performance benchmarks web-scraped from Tom's Hardware, and competitor printer search interest. Tested micro-hypotheses comparing internal and external signals using t-tests, then normalised conversion rates and benchmark scores into a composite performance score to classify products into High, Mid and Low tiers. A bonus section demonstrated out-of-core chunked processing on a multi-year Trends dataset to simulate memory-constrained big-data pipelines.
dataSources: CRM Sales Opportunities (Maven Analytics Data Playground)
Google Trends — GTXPro and sales-related keywords
GPU performance hierarchy (web-scraped from Tom's Hardware)
Multi-year Google Trends dataset (for out-of-core processing demonstration)

insights: The flagship product had effectively zero public search interest while the comparable generic category ('Sales Software') averaged 27.4 — a statistically significant visibility gap (t = 24.21). Strong internal conversion was masking the fact that nobody was finding the product organically.

The same pattern held against competitors: Canon printers averaged a Google Trends score of 73.0 versus roughly 1.0 for the company's MG printer line (t = 46.77, p ≈ 0.0000). Weak external visibility directly mirrored the MG line's weak CRM pipeline performance — two independent sources agreeing.

Technical superiority did not translate into sales. GTX Plus Pro had the highest benchmark score (~154) but the lowest conversion rate of the three GPU tiers (65%), while the technically weaker GTXPro and GTX Basic both converted at ~73.3% — a clear capability-versus-market-fit misalignment.

Deal duration and conversion were non-linear: short deals under 30 days converted best (66.4%), long deals over 90 days converted at 57.4%, but medium 30–90 day deals collapsed to 28% — suggesting two distinct winning patterns (quick wins and strategic wins) with stalled deals in between.

Conversion correlated more strongly with external market awareness (Canon printer interest, r = 0.43) than with raw technical performance (GPU score, r = 0.08) — market visibility mattered more than specifications.

recommendations: Invest in awareness (SEO/SEM, campaign-based marketing) for the flagship product — it converts well once in the funnel but is essentially undiscoverable, so the constraint is top-of-funnel visibility, not sales capability.

Reposition or retire the MG printer line. Two independent signals — internal pipeline performance and external search visibility — agree, which is a stronger basis for a portfolio decision than either alone.
Investigate why the highest-performing product converts worst: likely pricing, complexity, or messaging failing to communicate its technical advantage.
Treat medium-duration deals (30–90 days) as a pipeline health flag, not a normal stage — their 28% conversion suggests stalled rather than progressing opportunities.
Time campaigns to seasonal peaks identified in both CRM closures and public search interest, rather than running flat-line year-round activity.
projects.roi: Identified a measurable visibility gap on a well-converting flagship product, produced dual-source evidence supporting rationalisation of an underperforming product line, and surfaced a capability-versus-market-fit misalignment on the technically strongest product — insights none of which were visible from CRM data alone.

codeSnippets.title: Composite Performance Score & Product Tiering
codeSnippets.code:
# Normalise internal conversion and external benchmark to a common scale
merged['conv_norm'] = (
    (merged['conversion_rate'] - merged['conversion_rate'].min())
    / (merged['conversion_rate'].max() - merged['conversion_rate'].min())
)
merged['gpu_norm'] = (
    (merged['gpu_score'] - merged['gpu_score'].min())
    / (merged['gpu_score'].max() - merged['gpu_score'].min())
)

# Composite score blends internal performance with external capability
merged['composite_score'] = (merged['conv_norm'] + merged['gpu_norm']) / 2

# Segment into actionable tiers
merged['tier'] = pd.qcut(
    merged['composite_score'], q=3,
    labels=['Low Performer', 'Mid Performer', 'High Performer']
)

projects.title: Shared Prosperity & Social Well-being in New Zealand
projects.tagline: Recovering a corrupted socio-economic dataset, then testing how unemployment, inequality and housing tenure connect to wellbeing outcomes across NZ.
projects.org: Massey University — Data Mastery: Scripting, Databases and Data Privacy

businessProblem.context: Socio-economic indicators are usually reported in isolation — an unemployment figure here, a child poverty statistic there — which makes it hard to see how they move together. This project cleaned a deliberately corrupted New Zealand socio-economic dataset and combined it with the NZ General Social Survey 2016 to test whether these indicators are genuinely interconnected, and what that implies for policy.
goals: Recover a usable dataset from a corrupted source file with placeholder values, wrong data types and missing columns.
Test specific relationships: does unemployment relate to suicide rates, has the gender pay gap shifted post-2010, does inequality predict child poverty?
Bring in independent survey data to test whether housing tenure relates to life satisfaction.
painPoints: The source file contained '???' placeholder strings, columns misclassified as text despite holding numeric data, entirely empty columns, and duplicate rows — none of which could be assumed away.
Several indicators are heavily skewed, so mean imputation would have distorted them.
With only 37 usable rows after cleaning, the analysis had to be honest about what a dataset that size can and cannot support.

approach.methodology: Cleaned the corrupted dataset systematically: replaced '???' placeholders with proper NaN values, dropped fully-empty columns and duplicate rows, converted misclassified text columns to numeric types, and imputed missing values using the median rather than the mean — chosen deliberately because the skewed distributions would have pulled a mean-based imputation toward the outliers. Detected outliers using the Interquartile Range method rather than z-scores, since IQR is less influenced by the extreme values present in the data. Ran exploratory analysis and both Pearson and Spearman correlation matrices (Spearman to capture monotonic relationships that Pearson would miss), then hypothesis testing on the specific research questions, and a regression model predicting homeownership. Finally enriched the analysis with NZ General Social Survey 2016 data to compare life satisfaction between owner-occupied and non-owner-occupied households.
dataSources: Shared Prosperity dataset (deliberately corrupted source, provided by Massey University)

insights: Unemployment and suicide rates showed a clear positive correlation, and unemployment also tracked strongly with homeownership — supporting the view that economic stability and mental health outcomes are linked rather than independent.
Income inequality rose markedly over the period covered (correlation with year of 0.88), making it one of the strongest temporal trends in the dataset.
Child poverty correlated with both homeownership and unemployment, reinforcing housing stability as a plausible lever on poverty outcomes.

The NZGSS 2016 enrichment showed owner-occupier households reported higher life satisfaction than non-owner-occupiers — an independent dataset supporting the housing-stability-and-wellbeing link found in the main analysis.
Median-based imputation and IQR outlier detection materially changed the results versus naive mean imputation, given how skewed several of the indicators were.

recommendations: Treat housing stability as a cross-cutting policy lever — it correlates with child poverty, life satisfaction and mental health outcomes simultaneously, so it isn't only a housing issue.
Pair employment policy with mental health support, given the observed unemployment–suicide relationship.
Report both Pearson and Spearman correlations when indicators are skewed — several relationships that look weak linearly are considerably stronger monotonically.
Be explicit about sample size limits: with 37 usable observations, these findings are directional signals for further investigation, not conclusive causal estimates.
projects.roi: Recovered an unusable corrupted dataset into a clean analytical base, then produced cross-validated evidence — from two independent data sources — that housing stability connects to poverty, wellbeing and mental health outcomes across New Zealand.

codeSnippets.title: Robust Cleaning: Placeholders, Types and Outliers
codeSnippets.code:
# '???' is a placeholder for missing data - treat it as NaN, not a category
df.replace('???', np.nan, inplace=True)

# Several numeric columns arrived typed as object
numeric_cols = ['income_inequality_ratio', 'unemployment_rate',
                'loan_delinquency_percent', 'home_ownership_rate']
for col in numeric_cols:
    df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce')
    # Median, not mean - these distributions are skewed
    df[col] = df[col].fillna(df[col].median())

# IQR outlier detection - less sensitive to extremes than z-score
def flag_outliers_iqr(series):
    q1, q3 = series.quantile(0.25), series.quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    return (series < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (series > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)

projects.title: CRM Sales Database Design & Analysis (SQLite)
projects.tagline: Designing a 3NF relational schema for a B2B sales pipeline, then querying it to link deal outcomes with external market signals.
projects.org: Massey University — Data Mastery: Scripting, Databases and Data Privacy

businessProblem.context: CRM exports typically arrive as a set of disconnected flat files — accounts in one, agents in another, opportunities in a third — with duplicated fields and no enforced relationships. Analysing them repeatedly means repeatedly re-joining and re-cleaning. This project built a properly normalised relational database as the analytical foundation instead.
goals: Design a relational schema in Third Normal Form to eliminate redundancy and enforce data integrity across the sales pipeline.
Load, clean and insert CRM and external trend data into that schema with working key constraints.
Build analytical views and queries that answer real sales questions without re-deriving joins each time.
painPoints: Source CRM files used inconsistent column naming across exports and had no primary keys, so relationships had to be established rather than merely mapped.
External Google Trends data has no natural key linking it to CRM records — it aligns only by date and keyword, requiring a deliberate design decision about how to bridge internal and external data.

approach.methodology: Designed a six-table relational schema following Third Normal Form principles — accounts, sales_agents, products, opportunities, google_trends, and a consolidated merged_insights table — with primary and foreign key constraints enforcing referential integrity across product, account and agent relationships. Built the database in SQLite, standardising column names on load, generating surrogate keys where source data lacked them, and writing the creation scripts to be idempotent so the notebook could be re-run cleanly. Layered three analytical views on top of the base tables to support recurring queries on sales performance, product effectiveness and temporal trends without repeating join logic.
dataSources: CRM Sales Opportunities (accounts, agents, products, opportunities)

insights: Normalising to 3NF removed the repeated account and agent attributes that were duplicated across every opportunity row in the flat exports, reducing redundancy and making updates safe.
Foreign key constraints surfaced referential problems in the source data that flat-file analysis would have silently absorbed into incorrect join results.

Separating Google Trends into a standalone table — deliberately not force-joined to opportunities — kept the schema honest: external signals align by date and keyword, not by a genuine relational key.
Analytical views made recurring questions (conversion by product category, agent performance, trend alignment) a single query rather than a repeated multi-table join.

visualizations.title: Conversion Rate by Product Category
visualizations.description: Queried directly from the normalised database — GPU products convert at a substantially higher rate than printer products.

recommendations: Keep external signal data in its own table with explicit alignment logic rather than denormalising it into transactional records — it prevents implying a relationship that doesn't exist.
Use analytical views as the interface for recurring business questions, so query logic lives in one place rather than being re-written per analysis.
Write schema creation as idempotent scripts so the analytical pipeline is reproducible end-to-end.
projects.roi: Converted a set of disconnected CRM exports into a normalised, integrity-enforced relational database with reusable analytical views — turning repeated ad-hoc data wrangling into a queryable foundation.

codeSnippets.title: Schema Design with Referential Integrity
codeSnippets.code:
CREATE TABLE opportunities (
    opportunity_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id       INTEGER,
    agent_id         INTEGER,
    product_id       INTEGER,
    deal_stage       TEXT,
    engage_date      DATE,
    close_date       DATE,
    close_value      REAL,
    FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (agent_id)   REFERENCES sales_agents(agent_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(product_id)
);

-- Analytical view: conversion rate by product category
CREATE VIEW v_conversion_by_category AS
SELECT p.category,
       COUNT(*)                                        AS total_deals,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won_deals,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN o.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / COUNT(*), 2)                            AS conversion_rate
FROM opportunities o
JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;

projects.title: Practical Data Mining: Prediction, Classification & Association Rules
projects.tagline: Four applied modelling problems in R — regression trees, source attribution, survey clustering, and market-basket rule mining.

businessProblem.context: Different analytical problems demand fundamentally different techniques, and choosing wrongly costs accuracy. This project worked through four distinct problem types — continuous prediction, multi-class attribution, unsupervised segmentation, and association discovery — comparing competing methods on each rather than defaulting to one familiar approach.
goals: Compare linear and tree-based models for predicting a continuous outcome, and quantify the difference.
Attribute observations to their likely source using classification, and evaluate with balanced accuracy rather than raw accuracy alone.
Segment survey respondents without predefined labels, and mine association rules from transactional data using support, confidence and lift.
painPoints: Raw accuracy is misleading on imbalanced multi-class problems, so balanced accuracy was needed to evaluate honestly.
Association rule mining generates large numbers of trivially true rules; thresholds on support, confidence and lift were required to isolate genuinely informative ones.
Comparing models fairly requires consistent evaluation metrics across methods, not whichever metric flatters each one.

approach.methodology: Exercise 1: fitted both a linear regression and a regression tree (rpart) to predict ice thickness from spatial and temporal predictors, comparing them on RMSE. Exercise 2: built classification models to attribute campylobacter cases to their likely source, evaluating on both overall and balanced accuracy across classes. Exercise 3: applied clustering to New Zealand World Values Survey data to identify respondent segments without predefined labels. Exercise 4: used the Apriori algorithm on flag transaction data with a minimum support threshold of 0.023 (equivalent to 5 of 211 countries) and a confidence threshold, then filtered to rules with lift greater than 2 to isolate genuinely non-obvious associations from statistically trivial ones.
dataSources: Ice thickness training and test data (10,000 training observations)

insights: The regression tree substantially outperformed linear regression for ice thickness prediction (RMSE 0.5879 vs 0.8523) — the relationship was non-linear enough that a linear model left significant structure unexplained.

Model choice on the classification task made a decisive difference: the stronger model reached 95.5% accuracy versus 72% for the weaker one, with balanced accuracy confirming the improvement held across classes rather than coming from the majority class alone.

Clustering the World Values Survey produced four interpretable respondent segments differentiated primarily by age, education level, life satisfaction and self-reported health — with the first two dimensions capturing 49.8% of total variance.
Association rule mining surfaced clear colour co-occurrence patterns in national flags, with {Black} → {Red} showing the highest support (0.1745) among the rules examined.
Filtering to lift > 2 was essential — it separated genuinely informative associations from rules that were merely frequent because their component items were individually common.

visualizations.title: World Values Survey: 4-Cluster Segmentation
visualizations.description: Respondent segments identified via hierarchical clustering with complete linkage, projected onto the first two dimensions (49.8% of variance combined).

visualizations.title: Cluster Profiles Across Survey Variables
visualizations.description: Normalised variable distributions by k-means cluster (k=4), showing how the segments differ on age, education, life satisfaction, marital status and health.

recommendations: Test tree-based models alongside linear ones as standard practice — the RMSE gap here was substantial and would have been invisible had only linear regression been fitted.
Report balanced accuracy on any multi-class problem with uneven class sizes; raw accuracy can look strong purely from majority-class performance.
Always filter association rules on lift, not just support and confidence — high-support rules are frequently trivial.
projects.roi: Demonstrated method selection across four distinct problem types, with measurable comparisons at each step — including a 31% RMSE reduction from choosing a tree model over linear regression, and a 23-point accuracy gain from model selection on the classification task.

codeSnippets.title: Model Comparison & Association Rule Mining
codeSnippets.code:
# Compare linear regression against a regression tree
lm.model   <- lm(Thickness ~ ., data = ice.train)
tree.model <- rpart(Thickness ~ ., data = ice.train)

lm.train.rmse   <- rmse(ice.train$Thickness, predict(lm.model,   ice.train))
tree.train.rmse <- rmse(ice.train$Thickness, predict(tree.model, ice.train))
# lm: 0.8523   tree: 0.5879

# Association rules: support >= 5/211 countries
flag_rules <- apriori(flags,
                      parameter = list(support = 0.023,
                                       confidence = 0.5))

# Filter to genuinely informative rules
high_lift_rules <- subset(flag_rules, subset = lift > 2)
inspect(sort(high_lift_rules, by = "support", decreasing = TRUE)[1:5])

projects.title: Responsible AI in the Public Sector: Evaluating NZ's GenAI Guidance
projects.tagline: A critical evaluation of New Zealand's public-sector GenAI framework, testing it against a real deployment and finding gaps in data sovereignty, privacy compliance and cultural safeguards.
projects.org: Massey University — Data Mastery: Scripting, Databases and Data Privacy

businessProblem.context: New Zealand's Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service (GenAI) sets out how government agencies should deploy generative AI. But a framework only matters if it holds up against a real deployment. This evaluation tested it against Tourism New Zealand's 2023 use of ChatGPT-4 and sentiment analysis tooling to market Matariki internationally — a case that stress-tests the framework on data sovereignty, privacy law, and cultural safeguards simultaneously.
goals: Assess whether the framework holds up against current and emerging AI capabilities in a live public-sector deployment.
Test compliance against the Privacy Act 2020, Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations, and Māori data sovereignty under WAI 262.
Identify unintended operational and sociocultural consequences the framework doesn't anticipate, and propose specific reforms.
painPoints: The framework recommends bias audits but does not mandate them, so systemic gaps in training data pass through undetected.
Personal data collected to personalise campaigns was stored on offshore servers, creating a data sovereignty problem the guidance gives no direction on.
Liability is unclear when AI output causes harm — responsibility sits ambiguously between the agency designing the prompts and the model provider.

approach.methodology: Applied a structured four-lens evaluation to the framework: (1) fit with current and emerging AI capabilities, (2) legal and ethical protections under the Privacy Act 2020 and Te Tiriti o Waitangi, (3) unintended bureaucratic, operational and sociocultural consequences, and (4) comparative benchmarking against international regimes, notably the EU AI Act's third-party conformity requirements for high-risk systems. Each lens was tested against documented evidence from the Tourism New Zealand Matariki deployment rather than assessed in the abstract, then translated into specific policy, technical and legislative recommendations.
dataSources: NZ Government — Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service: GenAI (2023)
Privacy Act 2020 and Office of the Privacy Commissioner guidance
Documented Tourism New Zealand Matariki campaign deployment and public reporting

insights: The framework's strengths are real but shallow: transparency labelling and plain-language risk templates let a non-technical marketing team identify an offshore data storage problem and migrate to onshore infrastructure, satisfying Principle 12 of the Privacy Act 2020.

Compliance gaps were structural, not incidental. Personalisation data stored on offshore servers conflicted with Māori data sovereignty under WAI 262, and personalised campaign emails failed Privacy Act Principle 3 by not disclosing how cultural information would be used.

Making bias audits recommended rather than mandatory meant training-data bias went undetected — regional narratives were flattened and campaigns for distinct destinations became near-identical, eroding brand differentiation.

Compliance overhead has a measurable cost: a six-week compliance check delayed a campaign launch, and smaller agencies suspended AI programmes entirely rather than absorb the documentation burden — a distributional effect the framework does not account for.

Benchmarked against the EU AI Act, the same system would have required third-party conformity assessment as high-risk; under New Zealand's self-regulated model it received none, leaving affected parties without recourse.
recommendations: Mandate co-design with iwi rather than leaving consultation optional — the cultural failures traced directly back to their absence at design stage, not to model limitations.
Make bias audits compulsory rather than recommended. Voluntary audits systematically miss the failures they exist to catch.
Amend the Privacy Act 2020 to require onshore storage of Māori data, closing the sovereignty gap the current framework leaves open.
Require public accountability dashboards reporting demographic accuracy rates and error-correction timelines, so performance is externally visible rather than self-attested.
Introduce clear liability allocation between agency and model provider, so responsibility for AI-caused harm is traceable and actionable.
projects.roi: Produced a structured governance assessment identifying specific, actionable compliance gaps — offshore data storage conflicting with Māori data sovereignty, Privacy Act Principle 3 consent failures, and non-mandatory bias auditing — each mapped to a concrete legislative or operational remedy rather than a general recommendation.

projects.title: KPI & Governance Dashboard Reporting
projects.tagline: Consolidating fragmented multi-source data into standardised KPI dashboards across 80+ global agencies.

businessProblem.context: KPI, SLA, billing, and utilisation data for 7 Omnicom networks and 80+ global agencies was spread across separate systems (Replicon, Hive, Jira, Adobe Workfront), making reporting to senior leadership and clients a heavily manual process.
goals: Build standardised dashboards covering KPIs, SLA adherence, billing, and utilisation.
Automate the underlying data workflows to cut manual reporting effort.
Keep governance compliant through structured financial approval forms and scope trackers.
painPoints: Source data lived across four separate systems with no unified reporting layer.
Reporting was manual, which limited time available for actual analysis.
Quality breaches and delivery delays needed cross-team coordination to resolve.

approach.methodology: Built and maintained 50+ Power BI and Excel dashboards, automated SQL and Excel-based data workflows, and consolidated data from Replicon, Hive, Jira, and Adobe Workfront into structured reports for senior leadership and client-facing stakeholders. Also designed financial approval forms and scope trackers used as project contracts to keep governance compliant.

insights: Automating SQL and Excel-based workflows reduced manual reporting time by 70%.
Coordinating across Resource Management, Project Controllers, and Client Success teams resolved quality breaches and delivery delays more consistently.
recommendations: Keep the automated reporting workflow as the standard rather than reverting to manual consolidation.
Extend the same financial approval/scope-tracker governance model to new engagements as a default.
projects.roi: 70% reduction in manual reporting time, freeing team capacity for higher-value analysis across 7 networks and 80+ agencies.

projects.title: Recruitment Analytics Dashboard
projects.tagline: Uncovering hiring trends from 1,000+ survey responses to inform marketing and BD strategy.

businessProblem.context: Marketing and business development teams needed a clearer read on hiring trends and candidate engagement patterns than raw survey exports could provide.
goals: Analyse survey data from 1,000+ participants to surface hiring trends.
Build dashboards that make recruitment metrics usable for non-technical stakeholders.
Communicate findings clearly to a professional audience in real time.
painPoints: Survey data on its own didn't reveal actionable patterns without structured analysis.
Stakeholders needed insights presented live, not just as a static report.

approach.methodology: Analysed survey datasets from 1,000+ participants using SQL and Excel to uncover hiring trends and candidate engagement patterns, then built interactive dashboards to visualise the recruitment metrics.

insights: Interactive dashboards surfaced hiring trends and engagement patterns not visible in the raw survey exports.
Presenting findings live during LinkedIn virtual sessions made the insights more actionable for stakeholders in real time.
recommendations: Use the dashboard as a recurring input to marketing and business development planning, not a one-off analysis.
projects.roi: Enabled data-driven hiring-trend decisions for marketing and business development teams.
